title: Aberrations
lead: A real lens does not bring every ray to one focus as the thin lens equations say it should. This section describes chromatic aberration, coma and spherical aberration, and the ways optical systems reduce them while still gathering enough light for a bright image.
summary_html:
• Aberrations or image distortions can arise due to the finite thickness of optical instruments, imperfections in the optical components, and limitations on the ways in which the components are used.
  • The means for correcting aberrations range from better components to computational techniques.

figures.original_caption: (a) Chromatic aberration is caused by the dependence of a lens’s index of refraction on color (wavelength). The lens is more powerful for violet (V) than for red (R), producing images with different locations and magnifications. (b) Multiple-lens systems can partially correct chromatic aberrations, but they may require lenses of different materials and add to the expense of optical systems such as cameras.

(Figure 26.29) A coma is an aberration caused by an object that is off-center, often resulting in a pear-shaped image. The rays originate from points that are not on the optical axis and they do not converge at one common focal point. (Figure 26.30) Spherical aberration is caused by rays focusing at different distances from the lens.

exercises.prompt: List the various types of aberrations. What causes them and how can each be reduced?

answer.solution: Chromatic aberration is caused by the dependence of the index of refraction on wavelength, so a lens focuses violet closer than red; it is reduced by an achromatic doublet of crown and flint glass, or avoided by using mirrors. Coma is caused by an object off the axis, whose rays through different parts of the lens do not meet at one point; spherical aberration is caused by rays through the outer edges of a spherical lens focusing closer than rays near the axis; astigmatism is caused by a lens whose focus is uneven in different directions. These are reduced by specially shaped surfaces, graded index lenses, several elements that correct one another, and a smaller aperture that uses only the center of the lens, at the cost of brightness. Images can also be corrected by computing after they are collected.
